metadata.note: The Erie and North East Railroad and its two immediate neighbors, whose incompatible track gauges triggered the Erie Gauge War of 1853-54 -- one of the most colorful disputes in American railroad history, researched from Wikipedia and railroad-history sites. The Erie and North East (Erie, PA to the NY state line) was built to 6-foot broad gauge, while the Buffalo and State Line (Buffalo to the PA state line) and the Franklin Canal Company/Cleveland, Painesville and Ashtabula Railroad (Erie to Cleveland) both used the narrower 4'10' 'Ohio gauge' -- forcing Buffalo-Cleveland travelers to change trains twice within 20 miles at Erie. When the Buffalo and State Line's owners (who had quietly bought two-thirds of the Erie and North East's stock) forced a gauge conversion in Nov 1853, Erie's citizens rioted, tore up track, and even exchanged gunfire before the dispute was settled Feb 1 1854. All three predecessor companies merged into the Buffalo and Erie Railroad (1867) and then the Lake Shore Railway/Lake Shore & Michigan Southern Railway (1869), which Vanderbilt bought that same year, folding this corridor into the New York Central System -- see data/new_york_central.geojson's Water Level Route feature, which picks up this exact Buffalo-Cleveland corridor starting in 1869, so none of these three features has a segment past that year. Route geometry follows the real intermediate towns each railroad's own history describes, but is a simplified handful of waypoints, not surveyed track centerline. Era boundaries follow real corporate-history milestones (line openings, the gauge war itself, mergers); headway_min and avg_speed_kmh within each era are estimates, not sourced from real timetables. The Gauge War-era segments use an extreme headway_min (999999) as a placeholder to represent normal scheduled service being disrupted/suspended by the conflict, not a real number.
metadata.source: Wikipedia (Erie Gauge War, Lake Shore and Michigan Southern Railway, Cleveland Painesville and Ashtabula Railroad), eriehistory.blogspot.com, hmdb.org, american-rails.com (see conversation for citations)
metadata.line_label_audit: 2026-08-24: line labels normalised repo-wide to "<operating company>: <line name>" -- the company's common display name (legal suffixes dropped), then the line as a passenger would have known it, or its two terminals where the line carried no advertised name. Long intermediate station lists were reduced to endpoints. For features spanning several operators the company shown is the one that ran the line for most of its drawn years. See CLAUDE.md Rule 6.
metadata.geometry_audit: 2026-08-24: all three features re-traced from OpenStreetMap after the originals were found to cross Lake Erie. They had been 3-6 point sketches; the straight chord from Buffalo to Dunkirk ran 58.7 km over open water because the shoreline bulges between them. The corridor now follows the surviving lake-shore main line.
metadata.not_yet_sourced: The traced corridor runs about 12% longer than the mileages usually quoted for Buffalo–Erie (88 mi) and Erie–Cleveland (95 mi); the discrepancy has not been run down and may be terminal trackage, later realignment, or routing detours.

properties.line: Erie and North East: Erie, PA – NY state
properties.speed_source: estimated/blended across the line's history; unsourced

segments.note: Chartered Apr 12 1842, the Erie and North East Railroad finally opened Jan 19 1852: 19 miles of 6-foot broad-gauge track running east from Erie, PA to the New York state line, where it met the Buffalo and State Line Railroad's incompatible 4'10' (Ohio gauge) track -- forcing every Buffalo-Cleveland passenger and freight shipment to change trains twice within 20 miles. estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable
sources: Segment-level: this segment's own note carries the citation for its dates and service. Supporting references for the line:
Wikipedia (Erie Gauge War, Lake Shore and Michigan Southern Railway, Cleveland Painesville and Ashtabula Railroad), erie…

segments.note: The Buffalo and State Line's owners quietly bought two-thirds of the Erie and North East's stock, and on Nov 16 1853 announced they would re-lay its broad-gauge track to Ohio gauge. Erie's city council had already banned the new track from crossing city streets; the ensuing Erie Gauge War (Dec 7 1853 - Feb 1 1854) saw mobs tear up rails and ties, and a work-train official near Harborcreek shoot into a crowd on Dec 27 1853, knocking a man unconscious -- no scheduled trains ran through the disputed section during the worst of the fighting. estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable
sources: Segment-level: this segment's own note carries the citation for its dates and service. Supporting references for the line:

segments.note: The gauge dispute ended Feb 1 1854 when a train finally ran through Erie without a change; the line was now standard 4'8.5' gauge, matching its neighbors on both sides. estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable

properties.geometry_source: Real-traced from OpenStreetMap (ODbL) via Overpass, shortest-pathed with a strong preference for the way group OSM names the 'Lake Erie District' — the surviving Buffalo–Cleveland lake-shore main line that these three companies were consolidated into as the Lake Shore and Michigan Southern. 84% of the drawn length lies within 150 m of that line; the rest is terminal trackage at the Buffalo and Cleveland ends. GEOMETRY CORRECTED 2026-08-24: all three features here were 3-6 point sketches whose straight chords ran OUT OVER LAKE ERIE, because the shore bulges between the waypoints — the Buffalo–Dunkirk leg alone was one 58.7 km straight line across open water.
properties.geometry_quality: Real-traced, 325 points, median vertex spacing 85 m, longest step 1.6 km; every vertex sits on a mapped railway, so the line no longer leaves land. Traced 31.4 mi against the roughly 20 miles from Erie to the New York state line — it runs about 12% long across the whole corridor, which is unresolved: it may be terminal trackage at the ends, modern realignment, or small routing detours. LATER ALIGNMENT: this is the corridor as it survives today, not a verified 1850s alignment. Straight-line repair 2026-08-29: 1 ruled segment totalling 13 mi replaced with OpenStreetMap-traced rail geometry (see geometry_repairs for the OSM lines each one followed).

geometry_repairs.method: Overpass rail graph, 8.0 km corridor, Dijkstra, simplified to 3.0 m

properties.line: Cleveland, Painesville and Ashtabula: Erie, PA – Cleveland, OH
properties.speed_source: estimated/blended across the line's history; unsourced

segments.note: The Franklin Canal Company, chartered May 21 1844, built west from Erie, PA to the Ohio state line at 4'10' 'Ohio gauge' -- the same gauge the Buffalo and State Line used, and the gauge the Erie and North East would later be forced to adopt. The Cleveland, Painesville and Ashtabula Railroad, created Feb 18 1848 to build the Ohio side, completed the connection through to Cleveland Nov 20 1852. estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable
sources: Segment-level: this segment's own note carries the citation for its dates and service. Supporting references for the line:

segments.note: With the Erie and North East's incompatible broad gauge still in place to the east, western-gauge traffic could run unbroken from the Ohio line through to Cleveland, but still had to change trains at Erie during the Gauge War era. estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable

segments.note: The Cleveland, Painesville and Ashtabula bought the Franklin Canal Company outright June 20 1854, unifying the Erie-Cleveland corridor under one company just as the gauge dispute to the east was settled. estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable
